To view a copy of this license, visit http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . The move from reading to writing the human genome offers new opportunities to improve human health. The United States National Institutes of Health (NIH) Somatic Cell Genome Editing (SCGE) Consortium aims to accelerate the development of safer and more-effective methods to edit the genomes of disease-relevant somatic cells in patients, even in tissues that are difficult to reach. Here we discuss the consortium’s plans to develop and benchmark approaches to induce and measure genome modifications, and to define downstream functional consequences of genome editing within human cells. Central to this effort is a rigorous and innovative approach that requires validation of the technology through third-party testing in small and large animals. New genome editors, delivery technologies and methods for tracking edited cells in vivo, as well as newly developed animal models and human biological systems, will be assembled—along with validated datasets—into an SCGE Toolkit, which will be disseminated widely to the biomedical research community. We visualize this toolkit—and the knowledge generated by its applications—as a means to accelerate the clinical development of new therapies for a wide range of conditions. This Perspective discusses how the Somatic Cell Genome Editing Consortium aims to accelerate the implementation of safe and effective genome-editing therapies in the clinic. Subject terms Targeted gene repair Genetics research issue-copyright-statement © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Limited 2021 main Genetic factors contribute to most categories of human disease, including those that are inherited, infectious and malignant. It has therefore been a long-standing goal of biomedical science to develop a means to modify genomes within patients to correct disease-causing mutations, disable the genomes of invading pathogens, arm immune cells to attack tumours and enable countless other therapeutic opportunities. In some instances, gene addition can have therapeutic value, and gene therapy—the field that develops this approach—is experiencing ever-increasing success 1 . In many other cases, however, the genome of the patient must be edited to achieve therapeutic benefit. Genome editing broadly encompasses diverse technologies that can make many different genomic alterations in different contexts, and the topic has been the subject of recent and comprehensive reviews 2 – 4 . Several concepts in genome editing (Fig. 1 ) are central to the goals and strategies of the SCGE Consortium, which we describe in this Perspective. Over the past few decades, a steady progression of techniques and technologies that enable user-programmable genome editing has been introduced, tested, improved and implemented. These include homologous recombination, zinc-finger nucleases (ZFNs), meganucleases and transcription activator-like effector nucleases (TALENs) 5 – 7 . Most recently, engineered molecular machinery 8 – 15 derived from bacterial immune pathways—known as clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) and CRISPR-associated (Cas) proteins (CRISPR–Cas systems) 16 —have revolutionized genome editing 2 – 4 , in part because their target sequences can be simply programmed with easily designed RNA guides. Despite these promising advances, challenges remain before the transformative potential of therapeutic genome editing can be fully realized. Here we outline the goals and strategies of the SCGE Consortium, which has been established by the United States NIH to accelerate the development of solutions to many of these challenges. The NIH has allocated around US$190 million over 6 years in support of the SCGE Consortium, which now includes 72 principal investigators from 38 institutions that are pursuing 45 distinct but well-integrated projects. Until the past decade, the most prominent genome-editing platforms (ZFNs, meganucleases, TALENs and Cas9/Cas12a systems) relied almost exclusively on the realization 17 that the repair of nuclease-induced breaks in the genome can be exploited to induce genome edits (Fig. 1a )—either gene knockouts (through insertions or deletions generated by non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) or microhomology-mediated end-joining) or precise correction through homology-directed repair (HDR) 18 . Some editing events involve the insertion of vector-derived, ‘cargo’ sequences into the genome: natural examples of recombinases and transposases that can accomplish this task have been investigated for decades, and some (for example, lentiviral vectors) are being applied for gene therapy and genome editing 19 . In addition, some platforms can be implemented in partially or completely nuclease-inactive forms, by tethering to other effector proteins 20 . These strategies include base editing 21 (in which fused deaminase enzymes rewrite individual nucleotides without inducing double-strand breaks) 22 – 24 and prime editing (in which a fused reverse transcriptase introduces edits templated by an extended guide RNA) 25 . Nuclease-inactive forms can also be fused to enzymes to alter chromatin without changing the DNA sequence 26 , 27 (Fig. 1a ). molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: The primary activity context is therapeutic genome editing of somatic cells to correct disease-causing mutations, disable pathogens, and arm immune cells against tumors, encompassing various technologies like CRISPR-Cas systems, base editing, prime editing, epigenome editing, and mitochondrial DNA editing tools, along with their delivery and clinical translation.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Genome editing involves diverse technologies capable of various genomic alterations. Core mechanisms include exploiting nuclease-induced break repair (e.g., NHEJ for knockouts, HDR for precise corrections), insertion of cargo sequences (e.g., lentiviral vectors), and the use of nuclease-inactive forms fused to effector proteins for base editing, prime editing, or chromatin alteration. Specific approaches include gene knockout, excision of genomic regions, upregulating compensatory factors, removing exons or aberrant splice junctions, and sequence-specific alterations. CRISPR-Cas systems modify DNA sequences and epigenetic marks. Base editors (CBEs, ABEs) facilitate specific nucleotide transitions, while prime editing allows precise sequence and epigenetic edits. Epigenome editing can activate endogenous genes or reprogram cell phenotypes. Emerging technologies include nucleic acid analogues to evade immune detection, and new DNA manipulation systems (helicases, nucleases, transposases, recombinases) for improved efficiency and targeting. Peptide nucleic acids (PNAs) induce editing via triplex formation, and DddA-derived CBEs enable mitochondrial DNA editing. Delivery of these macromolecular components (e.g., Cas proteins, guide RNA, mRNA) to target cell nuclei is achieved via viral vectors (e.g., AAV) and lipid nanoparticles, including pre-formed CRISPR RNPs and virus-like particles. The SCGE Consortium advances these through integrated projects, rigorous independent validation, and establishing shared standards and toolkits for data integration, interoperability, and reproducibility to mitigate risks and extend therapeutic genome editing. Reporter animal models and non-invasive tracking methods are also being developed to detect and quantify editing events and cargo delivery.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: While 'efficiency' and 'precision' are critical, detailed dose-response comparisons are not extensively reported. Re-administration may be required for optimal cell population editing. Future strategies involve testing new delivery technologies in small and large animals, with a focus on enhancing viral vectors for high efficacy at lower doses via improved tissue-targeting. Dosing, safety, efficiency, and reagent distribution are critical preclinical considerations, especially in large animal models, with milestones tied to independent validation.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: Specificity, referred to as 'accuracy,' involves minimizing unintended edits at off-target sites and undesired modifications (e.g., large deletions, translocations) at intended loci. There is a recognized need to improve control over precise genomic changes, reduce unintended modifications, and ensure appropriate tissue targeting to prevent off-target activity in inappropriate tissues. Limitations exist for CRISPR-Cas effectors concerning editable regions and proximity to PAM sequences. The SCGE Consortium aims to enhance targeting capabilities and specificity, particularly for epigenome editors, which offer a potential advantage in reducing off-target mutations or genotoxicity. Delivery systems like nanoparticles are being developed with cell-type-specific homing, while current AAV systems have limited tissue tropisms. Reporter animal models and fluorescent proteins are designed to faithfully activate in targeted cell types, enabling detection of specific editing events.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: The target population includes patients with a wide range of conditions caused by genetic factors, such as inherited, infectious, malignant, blood and metabolic disorders, inherited forms of blindness and deafness, neuromuscular and neurological diseases, and specifically sickle cell disease and mitochondrial diseases (affecting ~1 in 5,000 people). The focus is on somatic cell genome editing, with germline editing explicitly excluded. Therapeutic applications target specific cell types and tissues, including respiratory epithelial cells, retinal cells, neurons in the brain, and primary T cells within human biological systems and organoids.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: The primary health implication is to significantly improve human health by correcting disease-causing mutations, disabling pathogens, arming immune cells against tumors, and achieving phenotypic rescue for various genetic diseases, including eliminating the need for blood transfusions in sickle cell disease. This involves accelerating the clinical development and translation of genome-editing technologies, enabling therapies for mitochondrial diseases, and addressing conditions through gene expression changes or cell phenotype reprogramming. The goal is to achieve therapeutically useful levels of genome editing, reduce development time and cost, minimize unintended biological effects, interpret mutation consequences, characterize editor/delivery component effects (e.g., immune responses), assess maladaptive responses, and produce assays for regulatory evaluation, ultimately enabling investigational new drug (IND) filings for a broadened spectrum of human therapeutic applications, especially in challenging somatic tissue contexts.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Genome editing offers significant protective benefit and therapeutic utility for a wide range of human diseases. However, there are substantial adverse risks associated with efficacy and safety, including toxicity, genotoxicity, immunogenicity (both innate and adaptive immune responses to editors or delivery vehicles), and unintended modifications such as off-target effects, vector integrations, large deletions, rearrangements, and insertional mutagenesis. Germline editing is explicitly considered an unacceptable outcome. Efforts are underway to mitigate these risks; for instance, epigenome-editing modalities show potential for eliminating off-target mutations or genotoxicity, and new gene editors are being designed to circumvent immune system detection, thereby reducing immunological responses. All potential adverse risks are actively being defined and mitigated.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The NIH SCGE Consortium is rigorously focused on developing, benchmarking, and validating genome editing approaches, including measuring modifications, defining functional consequences, and ensuring technology validation through third-party testing in small and large animals. Existing methods for off-target editing prediction and characterization are incomplete due to technological limitations, and animal models may not fully capture adverse responses. There is a critical need for new biological systems to measure safety and efficacy, common metrics, and standards for comparing technologies, along with robust analysis of PNA function across genetic loci. The SCGE program aims to generate in vivo reporter systems to quantify editing efficiency, specificity, and safety in target tissues. Reporter-animal models, fluorescent proteins, T cell platforms, and advanced imaging methods (PET, MPI, CEST MRI) are being developed for robust, sensitive, and longitudinal detection and quantification of editing events and delivery. Independent validation for all delivery technologies is explicitly required to ensure reproducibility, high-quality data, and interoperability within the SCGE framework, utilizing common standards, lexicons, and standardized data formats to facilitate investigational new drug (IND) filings.
